title: Logs, the digital and data management approach and the use of data
blurb: Explain the purpose of the daily log, lessons log and digital and data management approach, how data supports progress, who does what, and how progress links to the principles.
question: A project manager wants to note a sensitive concern that should not be openly visible to the team. Should it go in the issue register or the daily log?

teach.h: Two logs inside the project log
teach.body: PRINCE2 7 keeps its records in one project log: the daily log, the lessons log and the issue, risk, quality and product registers. The daily log is the project manager's informal diary: informal issues, actions, notes and observations. The lessons log is an informal repository of lessons for this and future projects. Both are set up in starting up a project.

head: Record
Holds
Practice
rows: Lessons for this and future projects
Products of a plan and their status

teach.h: The digital and data management approach
teach.body: Formally, this approach, part of the PID, describes how data and information will be created, used and managed across the project ecosystem, through the project lifecycle and afterwards. It covers matters such as security, privacy, storage, access, data quality and retention. It is one of the nine management approaches, agreed in initiating a project, and its home is the progress practice.

teach.caption: Data and systems support tracking and decisions; they do not set tolerances.

head: Role
Progress focus
rows: Sets project tolerances; decides project exceptions
Sets stage tolerances; decides stage exceptions
Sets WP tolerances; writes PM reports; keeps the log
Checkpoint reports; escalates WP breaches to PM

teach.h: Worked scenario: a social housing retrofit
teach.body: At Brookhaven Homes, project manager Sanjay Kapoor's PID includes a digital and data management approach saying tenant data is held on the housing system with restricted access and deleted after the warranty period. Sensor data from retrofitted homes flows automatically into a dashboard, so his highlight reports no longer need manual spreadsheets. A tenant's private complaint about a contractor goes in his daily log, not the open issue register.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) The daily log is informal; formal issues go in the issue register. (2) The lessons log records lessons as they arise; the lessons report passes them on. (3) The digital and data management approach is part of the PID and belongs to the progress practice. (4) Data and systems help track and forecast, but the management levels set the tolerances.

items: Daily log: PM's informal diary of issues, actions, notes and observations.
Lessons log: informal repository of lessons, set up in starting up a project.
Digital and data management approach (PID): how data is created, used and managed, during and after the project.
Data and automation support tracking, forecasting and presentation, not tolerance setting.
Progress supports manage by exception, manage by stages, learn from experience and tailoring.

summary: You can now explain the purpose of the daily log, the lessons log and the digital and data management approach, describe how data and systems support progress management, and link progress to roles and the principles.

A.q: What is the purpose of the daily log?
options: To record formal issues for the team to see
To record informal issues, actions and notes
To record lessons for future projects
To record products and their status
A.why: The daily log is the project manager's informal record of informal issues, actions, notes and observations.

whyNot.0: Formal issues are recorded in the issue register.
whyNot.2: Lessons are recorded in the lessons log.
whyNot.3: Products and their status are recorded in the product register.

A.q: What does the digital and data management approach describe?
options: How issues will be captured and changes controlled
How the project's benefits will be measured and reviewed
How data and information will be created, used and managed
How progress reports will be sent to the project board
A.why: It describes how data and information will be created, used and managed across the project ecosystem, through the lifecycle and afterwards.

whyNot.0: Capturing issues and controlling change is the issue management approach.
whyNot.1: Measuring benefits is set out in the benefits management approach.
whyNot.3: How and when reports reach stakeholders is covered by the communication management approach.

A.q: In which process is the lessons log set up?
A.why: The lessons log is set up in starting up a project, in the 'assess previous lessons' activity.

whyNot.0: Initiating a project sets up the registers, but the lessons log already exists by then.
whyNot.1: Controlling a stage uses the lessons log; it does not create it.
whyNot.2: Closing a project reviews the log to produce the lessons report.

B.q: A project manager hears a sensitive concern about a team member's conduct that should not be visible to everyone. Where should it be recorded?
B.why: Informal or sensitive issues, where open access would be inappropriate, are recorded in the daily log.

whyNot.1: The issue register is open to the team and holds formal issues.
whyNot.2: The lessons log records lessons, not sensitive issues.
whyNot.3: The concern has already arisen, so it is an issue, not a risk.

B.q:
Which two statements about the use of data in progress management are correct?
1. Stored past performance can be used to predict future performance.
2. Data and systems set the tolerances for each stage.
3. Automation can remove manual merging of reports from disparate sources.
4. Data should be presented in one fixed format for every stakeholder.
B.why: Stored data lets past performance predict future performance (1), and automation removes manual consolidation of disparate sources (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: management levels set tolerances.
whyNot.1: Both are false: tolerances come from management levels, and data is presented in stakeholders' preferred formats.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: information can be presented in each stakeholder's preferred format.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The digital and data management approach forms part of the [?].
B.why: Like the other management approaches, the digital and data management approach is part of the project initiation documentation (PID).

whyNot.0: The project brief is created in starting up a project, before the management approaches are agreed.
whyNot.2: Stage plans hold the detail of each stage, not the management approaches.
whyNot.3: The business case justifies the project; the approaches sit in the PID.

C.q: Which principle is supported by recording lessons in the lessons log and passing them on in the lessons report?
C.why: Seeking, recording and passing on lessons through the lessons log and lessons report applies learn from experience.

whyNot.0: Manage by exception is supported by tolerances and exception reporting.
whyNot.2: Focus on products is about defining and delivering products.
whyNot.3: Manage by stages is supported by stage-by-stage control and end stage reports.

C.q: Who typically maintains the registers in the project log, and who is responsible for them?
options: Project assurance maintains them; the executive
The team manager maintains them; the project board
Project support maintains them; the project manager
The business layer maintains them; the senior user
C.why: Project support provides administration such as maintaining the registers, while the project manager remains responsible for them.

whyNot.0: Project assurance is the board's independent check and is kept separate from support work.
whyNot.1: Team managers produce checkpoint reports; the board does not keep the project log.
whyNot.3: The business layer sits outside the project management team.

C.q: A board member suggests the new reporting dashboard should calculate and set stage tolerances. Why is this wrong, and who sets them?
options: Data supports decisions; the project board sets them
Dashboards are not allowed; the business layer sets them
Data is for closure only; the project manager sets them
Tolerances are fixed; the team manager sets them
C.why: Data and systems support tracking and decision-making, but the management levels set tolerances: stage tolerances are set by the project board.

whyNot.1: Dashboards are a valid use of data, and the business layer sets project, not stage, tolerances.
whyNot.2: Data supports progress throughout, and the project manager sets work package tolerances.
whyNot.3: Tolerances are set per plan level, and team managers work within work package tolerances.

reteach.title: A captain's notebook and the ship's records
reteach.question: How are a ship captain's private notebook and the official records like the daily log and registers?

blocks.body: A captain keeps a private notebook for passing thoughts, reminders and sensitive matters: that is the daily log. Official records that the crew can check are like the registers. A separate notebook of 'things to do better next voyage' is the lessons log. And the shipping company's rules on how voyage data is stored, shared and kept after the voyage are like the digital and data management approach.

blocks.text: The private notebook is not where formal problems are tracked for the whole crew: formal issues go in the issue register.

explain.body: The project manager's informal diary: informal issues, actions, notes and observations, including sensitive matters.

test.why: Informal issues are recorded in the daily log.

whyNot.0: The issue register records formal issues.
whyNot.2: The risk register records risks, which have not yet happened.

explain.body: An informal repository of lessons that apply to this or future projects, set up in starting up a project.

test.q: What does the lessons log hold?
options: Lessons for this and future projects
test.why: The lessons log is an informal repository for lessons that apply to this or future projects.

whyNot.1: Formal issues are held in the issue register.
whyNot.2: Products and their status are held in the product register.
whyNot.3: Quality activities and results are held in the quality register.

explain.body: Part of the PID: how data and information are created, used and managed across the ecosystem, during and after the project, including security and privacy.

test.q: Which practice is the home of the digital and data management approach?
test.why: The digital and data management approach belongs to the progress practice.

whyNot.0: Quality is home to the quality management approach.
whyNot.1: Organizing is home to the commercial management approach.
whyNot.3: Issues is home to the issue management approach.

explain.body: Data and technology support progress tracking and decisions; stored past performance helps predict the future; automation cuts manual work.

test.q: How do data and systems help progress management?
options: They decide whether to raise exceptions
They set the work package tolerances
They replace the project manager's judgement
test.why: Data and technology support progress tracking and decision-making and help predict future performance.

whyNot.0: People at each management level decide on exceptions.
whyNot.1: The project manager sets work package tolerances.
whyNot.2: Forecasts use data alongside judgement; data does not replace it.
